title: Palliative Measures
summary: Things can only get worse was a mantra of student life in the 1980s. Thatcherism was dystopic, a priori. Graduation was just a blip. We were all back in our berths at the union bar that evening. The tough thing about Chicago School monetarism was that it foreclosed on the futures that a university education […]
content:
Things can only get worse was a mantra of student life in the 1980s. Thatcherism was dystopic, a priori. Graduation was just a blip. We were all back in our berths at the union bar that evening. The tough thing about Chicago School monetarism was that it foreclosed on the futures that a university education was supposed to prep us for. On the upside, however, we were relieved of the burden of all the shoulds and oughts that traditionally came with a good degree. Self-worth seemed less about perfecting ourselves in the eyes of others and more about pursuing our own projects. Subsidised beer and holiday unemployment benefit were our proxies for 1960s psychedelics.

Compared to LSD, ego liquidation by beer is lagging and far less vivid. It took a lot of weak Hofmeister to tip students off the plateau of booze-induced social confidence and into oblivion.  I failed on both counts. My otroversion was more than a match for the feeble ABV. While others drank to the point of forgetting their own names, I’d be intense, focused and dull. The next morning, I would fill in the gaps of my colleagues’ memory lapses. Clearly self-awareness wasn’t the epistemological gold standard Descartes had made it out to be.

The other, it’s said, is always within us. I was from Lincolnshire, raised within a tribe of sensible, insular cagoule-wearing folk who eat proper sandwiches and are all-in on the mission to reproduce the past.  Could my talkative mother and present but completely unknowable father be squatting in my brain, living it small in a caravan? There were evenings in the bar when I was fearful that the beer goggles were morphing me into Joe 90, Gerry Anderson’s puppet school kid savant, yet the prospect of becoming my parents was much, much worse.

I was drowning in cheap beer by night and psychoanalysis by day. Freud, who habitually hangs us on the hook of family affaires, writes in Civilisation and its Discontents: “Life, as we find it, is too hard for us; it brings us too many pains, disappointments and impossible tasks. In order to bear it we cannot dispense with palliative measures.”

Freud’s “palliative measures” became a palliative in its own right.  Drinking, I told myself, was a means of coping with differences and separation. Neither remedy nor poison, as Plato had clear-headedly reasoned about something much more noble than lager. Better to show fidelity toward this emergent bookish sub-conscious than repress it. If I was to stay true to my desire and lessen anxiety, I needed to find a more abundant source of alcohol. One with a hobby element.

My first session wine was Plovdiv Bulgarian Cabernet Sauvignon. It was of the earth and of the people in a way my comrades’ cans of Royal Dutch Lager weren’t. Cheap, dark and tannic with a lingering aftertaste of iron curtain. I liked the fit. I could stay in the effervescent flow of just-graduated existence while  nurturing this fragile new pastime into something more enduring.

Cabernet Sauvignon became a go to. The great acceleration in global wine production was underway and Australia and California both provided impressive versions of the variety. I tried spending a bit more on bottles and was, for the most part, rewarded.  Opus was never intended to be the opium of the people (opioids do that job), but California was a blue state, and with Bob Hawke in The Lodge both it and Bin 707 made the weekend cut.

I bought a copy of Hugh Johnson’s Wine Atlas and began experimenting with Bordeaux. My life took on the mantle of a vinous ouroboros. I poured myself into wine education, heart and soul (and liver), enrolling on a couple of WSET courses, then I poured this knowledge into myself every evening. There was all-round relief when I finally took to spitting, repulsive and expulsive as it is, which suggests this positive feedback loop had a negative impact on those around me. I became a tasting machine. Wine was reified into an object discoverable through its sensory qualities rather than its mood changing effects.

To properly get a feel for the vastness of space you need to escape the Earth. The purview of stars and planets multiplies once you’ve out-muscled gravity. Wine education can have a similar dynamic. You either reach escape velocity and acknowledge how little you know, or you stay on the surface, anchored to what’s familiar.

“I know what I like” is crushing for those of us who have climbed the ladder of wine education. It’s the certainty that really grates. When the Vintners’ Company set up the Institute of Masters of Wine in the 1950s, presumably their aim was to structure wine education around dependable English merchant types. A commonwealth of wine with London at its heart. Such rational exuberance may have seemed justified when the limits of production were so fixed, yet once the rest of the world got in on the act the push for omniscience faltered. In the expanded universe of wine there is no unitary position, no end, there are only points of departure, unless you’re that bigot with the stacked trolley of BOGOF Malbec.

I’m trying to resist the urge to go all Lincolnshire and put decades of separation between me and my desire, because nearly everything that existed back in the 1980s isn’t worth a rerun.  To be positive for a moment, as students we weren’t sluiced into debt, and holidays were covered by the DHSS if you felt there were better options than slogging through character building night shifts at the pea factory.  Nor did we have to dodge the government draft that wants to turn all able sixth formers into engineers. There was an opportunity to jink like knights across the chessboard rather than be pawns that can be shuffled from square to square. Just as teenagers have to familiarise themselves to new body settings, so an educated mind needs time to evaluate possibilities. Subjectivation isn’t a switch.

We can only interpret our desire after the fact. Retrospectively. Exchanging pleasure for enjoyment isn’t just semantic. The latter has an arc of difficulty as well as satisfaction. For what cause other than desire would I have taught myself chemistry, botany and geology?

The shift from beer to wine 40 years ago was a decisive event. I peeled off into the atomised world of producers and grape varieties then slowly pieced things together in some small ways that seemed to work as work, theses and friendships. I count myself lucky to have lived in the age of Paul Draper; even met nice South Africans. “I’ve known adventures, seen places you people will never see. I’ve seen it. Felt it!”  To quote Roy Batty.

Photo by NASA on Unsplash

title: A Performance Art
summary: Susannah Cibber was a terrific singer, by all accounts. Handel gave her the contralto solos in Messiah, and she had a great acting career as well: she became the highest paid actress in England. What did she sound like? Not the most polished of singers by contemporary accounts, but very expressive, very moving, very sweet, […]
content:
Susannah Cibber was a terrific singer, by all accounts. Handel gave her the contralto solos in Messiah, and she had a great acting career as well: she became the highest paid actress in England.

What did she sound like? Not the most polished of singers by contemporary accounts, but very expressive, very moving, very sweet, and with a wide vocal range. And that’s pretty much all we have to go on.

Nor do we know what ancient musical instruments sounded like, or what the music sounded like in Greek theatres. Prehistoric bone flutes have been discovered, and played: you can hear them online. They sound rather modern. But what music was played on them we do not know.

Nor do we know what wine tasted like in the past. Wine, like music, is a performance art, but unlike music now it can’t be recorded. The second taste can be different to the first, even from the same glassful, and especially if food is involved.

And so we’re obsessed with pinning it down, writing yard-long tasting notes most of which convey nothing for all their length, except how many adjectives we know. The more tasting notes from different tasters you put together to try and arrive at a consensus, the more you end up with the information that it tasted like, well, wine. Apart from the few seconds in which it is in your mouth, or the scent in your nose, wine is virtual. It is either past or future.

Which do we enjoy more? Memory or anticipation? It works for mice too, apparently. According to a report in The Times the other day, baby mice exposed to the smell of citronella while living in the lap of luxury (cornflakes, running wheels, playmates) loved the smell of citronella in adulthood. Those who did not associate the smell with pleasurable experiences were indifferent to it later. Which, as an aside, is useful information for anyone wanting their Christening gift of a case of 2024 Port to be properly appreciated by its recipient: wave a glass of good Vintage under their noses while they’re having a happy time pulling the legs off their enemies on Tik Tok, or whatever children do for amusement now. In future years those memory networks will spring into action every time Port comes their way and they’ll be raiding your cellar long before you’re dead enough to hand them the key. The wine trade’s problems will be solved for another generation.

Think of Chaucer’s Pardoner, being transported to ‘Spaigne, right at the toune of Lepe’ by three draughts of ‘wyn of Spaigne’. Or taste a Very Very Old Port – perhaps a Tawny, perhaps a white like Taylor’s latest release: it’s freighted with memories, and thanks to photography they don’t even have to be our memories. Nobody under 85 remembers the Douro Valley 80 years ago, which is the average age of the wine; but we’ve seen photographs. Photography, I contend, has done more to increase the enjoyment of wine by association than anything else. Photographs link us to the shooting parties, the picnics, the basking river (not yet dammed), the proudly shown new cars, the dresses, the improbable suits in hot summers. The taste of wine can transport us to somewhere we never were.

An even older wine – one older than photography – is weirdly less vivid. I’ve tasted Madeira from the 18th century, and I told myself, as I pinched myself, that this was made when Marie-Antoinette was on the throne of France! This was made when George III was alive! But the thrill was less because the references were less personal. A faded photograph of a group of people one never knew looking faintly uncomfortable in a spot one has never visited strikes far more of a chord than the formal relics of a century or more earlier. Momentary experience, caught on film, responds to the momentary experience of the wine.

A friend of mine will hunt down obscure bottles of Burgundy and take them to their vineyard to drink them. It’s fun, but literal. If I taste Mouton-Rothschild I’m less likely to be transported back to particular corners of that vineyard, and more likely to remember Philippine and the time I went to interview her in Paris and she was hopelessly late and I was starving hungry and the maid brought some petits fours and I wondered how many I could eat without looking desperate. Give me a taste of Mouton-Rothschild and I think of those petits fours.

Fungal networks in soil spread out way beyond the roots of a plant to reach other plants, other fungal networks. A single photograph of a Spanish peasant with a wineskin extends our memory networks to a culture we never knew. Rather as an oak tree might depend in winter on networks stretching for miles for its nutrition, so wine depends on the links provided by forms that extend way beyond memory to sustain its glamour, and to give the moments of tasting a resonance far beyond a few adjectives.

The indifference, the quick snap of the camera is far more effective in this than the weighted imagination of the painter. Vladimir Nabokov in Speak, Memory mentions somebody looking at home movies made before his birth: ‘He saw a world that was practically unchanged – the same house, the same people –and then realised that he did not exist there at all and that nobody mourned his absence.’

The photographs in The Australian Ark, Andrew Caillard MW’s monumental history of Australian wine, are extraordinarily evocative. My copy of Volume I falls open at a picture from the 1870s: a young woman in a torn, shabby dress and worn shoes standing composedly in the doorway of the Gulgong Tobacconist in NSW, which sold cricketing equipment – ‘bats, balls, stumps & gloves of every description’, tobacco, ‘cigars of the best brand’, bread for 4d a loaf (the sort that would be £6 now) and ‘Colonial Wine’s’ [sic].

Volume II of The Australian Ark has a 1942 photograph of ‘Australian Army officers sampling Champagne intended for the messes of the AIF in the Middle East’: Charles Heidsieck, cases stencilled ‘Zone Franche Privée, Beyrouth’, the officers – ciggie in mouth, paper cup in hand, trying not to laugh. It takes my thoughts in more directions than I can count: my father in the British Army, my uncle in the Australian Air Force, Beirut and the long and cosmopolitan history of Levantine culture, Champagne, Dad’s Army, pinewood wine boxes, forest fires in the Landes…

There is a portrait of Susannah Cibber, by Thomas Hudson, in 1749. It’s a very nice portrait of a young woman, not a beauty, dressed in heavy satin with pearls in her hair, her face the anonymised female face of the day. It would look very good over a fireplace on in a panelled hall. She, like a bottle of wine, was a performance artist. Like unrecorded music or wine in the bottle, she is mute.

Photo by Kyle Head on Unsplash

title: Hand In Hand
summary: Rowan Hooper’s new book, Togetherness, is a fascinating study of symbiosis, what he calls a “neglected silo” of scientific research. The subject might sound a bit geeky and pointy-headed, but it’s central to the way that nature works. To anyone brought up on Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species, or who has watched an […]
content:
Rowan Hooper’s new book, Togetherness, is a fascinating study of symbiosis, what he calls a “neglected silo” of scientific research. The subject might sound a bit geeky and pointy-headed, but it’s central to the way that nature works.

To anyone brought up on Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species, or who has watched an hour of Nature’s Deadliest Animal Showdowns narrated by a whispering Sir David Attenborough, the idea that nature favours co-operation and collaboration over conflict and the survival of the fittest will seem counterintuitive. An unashamed Darwin fan, Hooper says that the notion that competition is the only driver of evolution is incorrect.

There’s a human element to this too, although it goes against the precepts of capitalism and “social Darwinism”. “We live on a symbiotic planet,” he writes, “we are a symbiotic species, and only together will we thrive.” Hooper argues, convincingly, that “symbiosis blurs the meaning of individual”, a message for our times perhaps.

The book contains numerous examples of symbiosis in action, from lichens to coral, ants to orchids, wasps to figs. Different species seek out and, invariably, find the right partner. What’s more, they communicate with each other at some non-verbal level. Far from being static, the relationship is fluid and evolves, as all good relationships must.

Vines do not feature in the book. I attended a lecture that Hooper gave in London recently and he admitted that they are not his area of expertise. But in a recent podcast I did with Katia Nussbaum of San Polino in Brunello de Montalcino, I was fascinated to learn about her experiments with “vitiforestry”, which is another example of symbiosis.

The link between trees and grape vines is older than wine itself. Wild vines are essentially creepers, or climbers, seekers of light to drive photosynthesis. Until they were domesticated, they used trees to find it. You can still see this form of arboreal viticulture in Chile – Bouchon’s País Salvaje label has a drawing of a picker on a ladder – and especially Bolivia’s Cinti Valley. Trees provide a form of natural trellis for the vine, as well as shade and frost protection. The downside is that they compete for water – a concern with climate change – and may bring new pests and diseases to vineyards.

But the positives seem to outweigh the negatives, not least in terms of biodiversity. At Cheval des Andes in Mendoza, the multinational LVMH, not a company to waste money for the sake of it, has planted 2,000 trees among the rows of vines at its estate in Las Compuertas since 2021 to create what it calls a “polyculture”.

Back in Montalcino, Katia Nussbaum and her family have incorporated maple trees into one of their vineyards to see if symbiosis occurs. The whole estate is surrounded by forest, but now she’s taken the connection a stage further.

Thanks to the work of writers such as Suzanne Simard and Peter Wohlleben, we know that trees communicate with each other through networks of mycorrhizal fungi. They also work together as a community, with older trees nurturing the younger ones with food and water. Healthy vineyards, too, have their fungal network. Is this more developed in older, more established parcels? Are organic, biodynamic or regenerative forms of agriculture more likely to allow it to flourish? The answer is almost certainly yes.

Well-farmed vineyards are alive. I once walked through a biodynamic vineyard in Burgundy with the late Anne-Claude Leflaive and it was like treading on a thick carpet; a chemically treated one next door was a stretch of concrete by contrast.

Talking to Katia made me think about terroir, which is not an easy term to explain. It’s sometimes called a “three-legged stool” in France, combining soil/geology, climate and a human element, with knowledge passed down through the generations. Of course, terroir is considerably more complicated than that. Katia describes what’s happening in vineyards as a cat’s cradle, “its strings held not only by human hands but by all the organic and non-organic elements whose togetherness gives rise to the living whole”. I think she’s right. Some of these relationships we understand; most we don’t. Yet soil health is —and should always be—recognised as a vital part of terroir.

Are the vines, too, communicating with each other, working together as a unified entity? Does terroir think, as it were? Are the fungal networks of trees and vines stronger than the sum of their parts? “We don’t know,” she says. “All we’re doing is asking questions.” The right questions in my view.

Originally published in Harpers Wine & Spirit; photo by Sebastian Dumitru on Unsplash

title: Michelin And The Death Of The Wine Guide
summary: It was entirely predictable that Michelin’s new venture into wine would trigger huffy French recriminations. Its Wine Selection Burgundy 2026, launched this month, awarded nine producers the top accolade of three grapes, another 20 vignerons two grapes, and 33 one grape. A further 32 were merely “selected”. Mais putain! They only gave Domaine Arnoux-Lachaux one […]
content:
It was entirely predictable that Michelin’s new venture into wine would trigger huffy French recriminations. Its Wine Selection Burgundy 2026, launched this month, awarded nine producers the top accolade of three grapes, another 20 vignerons two grapes, and 33 one grape. A further 32 were merely “selected”. Mais putain! They only gave Domaine Arnoux-Lachaux one grape? The celebrated Vosne-Romanée house publicly demanded its removal from the guide. But the row says something more fundamental about the demise of what has been one of the vinous world’s key organising systems: the wine guide.

Michelin’s new guide had attracted criticism before publication. When first announced last December, the publisher said its selections would “spotlight wine estates and producers across different regions of the world” – but it’s not clear when they’ll get around to rating anywhere outside France. Ribera del Duero? I wouldn’t bother keeping dates free, compañeros. Martinborough? Mais c’est où, ça?

Their method has been criticised too: it rates producers rather than wines, based on estates’ vineyard management, consistency and so on. Whatever the fairness of this, it doesn’t seem like a very useful product for consumers, at least compared to the obvious French competitor, the Guide Hachette des Vins, now in its forty-second edition and generally regarded as the bible of the French wine industry.  Hachette rates individual cuvées from one to five, plus “coup de coeur” judges’ favourites.

It’s not clear how Michelin worked: Arnoux-Lachaux say they weren’t visited and that they stopped submitting wines for reviews years ago. The suspicion is that Michelin involved the Wine Advocate: it purchased a 40% share in Parker’s publication in 2017, acquiring it entirely in 2019. Trying to sweat that asset to expand the Michelin empire beyond restaurants and hotels could make sense. Might William Kelley, WA’s Editor-in-Chief and Burgundy specialist, have had a hand? He raved about Domaine Jean-Marc & Thomas Bouley‘s 2023 Pommard 1er Cru Les Rugiens Hauts – rated 100 points – months before the not-very-grand Volnay producer won “three grapes”. Michelin responded to this suggestion by saying simply that their judging team “brings together seasoned wine specialists and newly recruited inspectors… They are all seasoned professionals in the sector – former sommeliers, specialised critics or production experts.”

These might look to many drinkers like arcane squabbles in the rarified world of fine wine. But the real significance of Michelin’s wine venture is that it definitively marks the end of the consumer wine guide as we know it.

Mapping the best wines for buyers began with Cyrus Redding’s A History and Description of Modern Wines (1833). One might argue that Bordeaux’s 1855 classification did something similar – though the intended audience was still largely merchants and professionals. Wine advice for ordinary drinkers emerged later and more gradually from food, etiquette and travel writing.

Consumer-oriented wine publications as we’d understand them today first appeared only in the 1970s. The mid-late decade brought both Decanter and Wine Spectator magazines, as well as Hugh Johnson’s Pocket Wine Book (1977) and Parker’s Wine Advocate. The first recommendation-based handbooks arrived in 1980: Jancis Robinson’s Which? Wine Guide 1981 and John Platter’s first South African Wine Guide. France’s Guide Hachette des Vins and James Halliday’s Australian Wine Companion came out soon after, followed elsewhere, for instance, by José Peñin’s eponymous Spanish wine bible (1990).

There was always a problem, however, with print guides to wines on sale, especially if they specified particular shops: the books were out of date before they hit the shelves. This gap was made most obvious by the genre’s apotheosis, Malcolm Gluck’s Superplonk, first appearing in 1991 on the back of his Guardian column of the same name. But from the mid-1990s, consumers were getting access to a far more up-to-the-minute source of information – the internet. Gluck’s printed guide died an unlamented death in 2006.

Meanwhile the vast expansion of the wine world in the four or five decades since the advent of consumer guides means that, at least in places like the UK that import from everywhere, there’s far too much variety for any single guide to cover everything. Technological change may tame this field but it raises different dilemmas. The next iteration of the wine guide will, it seems, be powered by AI: even now, we face a growing tide of (mostly pseudo-) AI-driven apps telling people what to buy. But as with the internet’s impact on every other facet of criticism, it raises the urgent question: whose advice is this? Whose opinion?  Can we trust it? AI wine apps are only as good as what people put into them.

Which brings us back to the value of guides written by human authors, whether anonymous or not. Many country-specific guides like Platter and Peñin retain their authority today, and have the virtue too of availability online as websites (and as an app, for Platter) to stay up to date. Most of Tim Atkin MW’s online reports have a narrower focus (regions or single countries) but greater depth. But while such guides are vital for wine professionals, and have cachet with producers, it’s questionable how many consumers rely on them, even the electronic versions. (Plenty do! Ed.)

This is the wine media world into which Michelin has launched itself. Inclusion in its selections probably confers some cachet, as the reactions to poor ratings suggest. But I can’t see many drinkers using it – not least because few of the Burgundian producers named welcome non-trade guests, let alone stooping to anything as déclassé as wine tourism.

And the Gallic focus? As with restaurants, it would be naïve to expect much from Michelin beyond French chauvinism and thinly-veiled snobbery. If the wine selections do ever venture outside l‘Hexagone, expect something as confused and tokenistic as the star awarded to Mexico City taco stand El Califa de León (though I can confirm their $2.50 tacos are superlative.) As for that wine guide that you pull out in a shop: RIP – it was fun while it lasted. But I’m not hailing the wine app as the future just yet.

 Photo by Nick Fewings on Unsplash; Andy Neather blogs at https://aviewfrommytable.substack.com/

title: The Yang Of Greek Wine
summary: By now this is so well-known that repeating it enters broken record territory. The biggest story for Greek wine the past 20 years has been the rise of Assyrtiko. From a Santorinian oddity / best-kept secret to international fame, it did more than any other grape variety to put Greek wines on the map. It […]
content:
By now this is so well-known that repeating it enters broken record territory. The biggest story for Greek wine the past 20 years has been the rise of Assyrtiko. From a Santorinian oddity / best-kept secret to international fame, it did more than any other grape variety to put Greek wines on the map. It also built a certain perception of, and expectation from, Greek white wine: it should be sharp, acidic, mineral. Hellenic varieties that have a passing moment in the spotlight, from Vidiano to Roditis, Moschofilero to Robola, seem, at least partially, to want to play dauphin to Assyrtiko’s king.

Or at least, that’s the story abroad. I periodically write about the disconnect between the international and local market, a difference that is more pronounced in Greece than perhaps any other wine-exporting nation in the world. And, if I had to pick the biggest white wine story in Greece the past 20 years, I would be split between two options. One would be the expansion, explosion even, of Assyrtiko, not as a top-quality wine (we have known that well before the rest of the world caught up), but as something planted across the country. But I would be equally likely to go for something else: the rise of Malagousia. (The pedant in me wants to transliterate it correctly, i.e. Malagouzia, and I salute the producers that do it, but this fight is one of those I had to give up. I surrender to the hoi polloi.)

Malagousia comes with a cool, if not uncommon, story. It was saved by the very brink of extinction from a fortuitous meeting of minds in the late-70s between an agriculturalist, a viticulture professor, a winery owner, and the then young firebrand winemaker Vangelis Gerovassiliou. Delivering results almost immediately, it was soon planted by Gerovassiliou in his own vineyards, eventually becoming a major element in his landmark Estate white. Yet, in the international variety-focused 1990s, and the somewhat ambivalent 2000s, Malagousia was far from dominant: for a very long time Gerovassiliou was the go-to name for the variety. (Plus, for the well-informed, Roxane Matsa, arguably the most undersung figure in modern Greek wine).

And then, some time around the late noughties, this started to change. New labels started to emerge. Producers were planting it in places well outside Macedonia, where it had found a home (its actual origins are meant to be on the western side of central Greece). As Greek consumers were becoming both more educated about wine and more willing to make their native varieties the protagonists, Malagousia started climbing in popularity and impact.

For those who know Greek wine primarily via grapes such as Assyrtiko or Moschofilero, this might come as a surprise. In its most succulent versions, it wouldn’t be an exaggeration to call Malagousia the Yang to Assyrtiko’s Yin. Rich, generous, with summer and tropical fruits, it hovers somewhere between Semillon, Viognier, and Muscat, without being quite like any of them. In its drier, more herbal incarnations, it comes with echoes of Viura or Garnacha Blanca, but, again, being its own thing.

Why does this fit the Greek palate so well? Because, in many ways, it is the perfect summer wine: ideal with lighter food, such as most types of seafood, salads, or grilled vegetables, but equally comfortable with a plate of fruit. In its more glou-glou takes, it makes for easy drinking. I bow to no one in my love for Assyrtiko, but for me to pour it, it has to be good. I can offer someone a glass of an undistinguished Malagousia, however, and still feel I made a safe bet.

People back home seem to share my views. By 2020, it had caught up with Chardonnay in vineyard acreage, and had Moschofilero in its sights. I don’t have more recent data, but I wouldn’t be surprised if they’re about even by now. The number of producers working with it has certainly skyrocketed. So, take the recommendations below as a starting point: there are many more to explore – and even more to come.

title: Marketing Natural Wine
summary: I recall a conversation I had with one of the new people I met when I first moved to Madrid. She’d found out that I worked in wine. “In wine?” she said with excitement. “There’s a great wine bar in Lavapiés you must try! They sell natural wines, it’s really good.” I took out my […]
content:
I recall a conversation I had with one of the new people I met when I first moved to Madrid. She’d found out that I worked in wine. “In wine?” she said with excitement. “There’s a great wine bar in Lavapiés you must try! They sell natural wines, it’s really good.” I took out my phone, pinned it on the map, noted in parenthesis that it’s a natural wine bar. In the two years since, I haven’t been once.

I don’t know what the rest of the wine industry thinks of the natural wine movement, and I don’t speak for anyone else, but as for me, well, what is an un-natural wine anyway? Where do we draw the line? Does the vine itself need to crush its grapes and bottle its own juice?

Perhaps my scepticism stems as much from the movement’s nebulous definition as it does from the foul wine I was served in a trendy wine bar in Shoreditch, or from the sommelier insisting that it was supposed to taste like that, that there was nothing wrong with the wine. The implication, of course, was that there was something wrong with me, my palate, that I simply didn’t understand natural wine. It was ten years ago. Since then, natural wines have become cleaner, or so I’m told, and it’s no longer natural wine; it’s low-intervention wine.

And you’d be wrong to think this is a piece to disparage natural wine. Quite the opposite. Despite my personal prejudice, I’ve discovered that some of the finest wines I’ve tasted have been marketed as natural — Gravner being an obvious example — and there are many others I’m eager to try, among them Chris Boiling’s Crazy Experimental Wines, which we’ll come back to shortly.

This is an exploration of natural wine’s remarkable success, and whether some of the factors behind that success can be applied to the rest of the wine world.
In fact, natural wine not only is the leading opportunity in wine according to IWSR’s Opportunity Index — which measures the strongest market opportunities for alternative wine categories, weighted by the size of each country’s wine-drinking population — but it is also one of the industry’s fastest-growing segments. Estimates from DataIntelo Consulting suggest the global natural wine market is expanding at around 13% annually, an impressive feat at a time when the broader wine market is struggling to grow.

The evidence extends beyond bottles produced. Natural wine bars continue to proliferate across major cities in Europe (Paris alone has 600, according to French app Raisin), North America and Asia, signalling that the movement has firmly entered the mainstream.

And perhaps most remarkably, natural wine has achieved what much of the wine industry has struggled to do: capture the imagination of the notoriously elusive Gen Z consumer.

As I’ve already hinted, what natural wine remains surprisingly ill-defined. Perhaps that’s part of its appeal. An idea is often more powerful when different people can project different meanings onto it. Even Georgia, one of the first countries to legislate a definition of natural wine, defines it vaguely as “wine produced through the spontaneous fermentation of organically grown grape must” without “the use of oenological practices and substances otherwise permitted under general winemaking regulations, with the exception of sulphur dioxide, which must be limited to a maximum concentration of 40 mg/l.”

Ah! Sulphur dioxide—the Enemy, with a capital E, that the natural wine movement has set out to slay. In the public imagination, mild wine intolerance is often blamed on sulphur dioxide, a belief reinforced by plenty of anecdotal evidence but very little scientific support.

In her Master of Wine research paper, What is the Relationship Between the Use of Sulphur Dioxide and Biogenic Amine Levels in Wine?, Sophie Parker-Thomson MW argues that the likely culprit behind adverse reactions in some wine drinkers is a group of compounds known as biogenic amines (BAs), which are naturally present in all fermented foods and beverages. Her findings turn the sulphur dioxide narrative on its head. Wines with no added SO₂—or with sulphur added only late in the winemaking process — were found to contain the highest levels of biogenic amines. Unsurprisingly, those conclusions caused no small amount of discomfort among supporters of natural wine, yet they did little to challenge the sulphur dioxide myth, as the research never made its way into the public consciousness.

So, sulphites aside, if there is no formal definition, how do you identify a natural wine when browsing the shelves of a wine shop or supermarket? As former United States Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart famously said of obscenity, “I know it when I see it”— the same could be said of natural wine.

In fact, while wine professionals continue to argue over what natural wine is and isn’t — or what low-intervention wine really means—the movement has succeeded in capturing the imagination of the average wine consumer. Why is that? Is it the places where it’s sold? The people behind it? The labels? The messaging? Probably all of the above.

Orwell wrote of his job reviewing books that most of them are so bad that, in nine cases out of ten, the only honest review would be: “This book is worthless.” It made me think that in wine, the opposite is true. “This wine is good” likely describes 90% of the wines, which arguably makes the job of a wine critic even harder than that of a book critic. What is there to say when a wine is good? Good, but not great. Good, but not particularly interesting. Well-made, sound, solid, like all the rest… What is there to object to? Nothing — other than, perhaps, that in a sea of identical wines, it’s just really hard to sell.

The final step in wine production is the first from the consumer’s point of view: the packaging.

Natural wines have cool names like Seggs with My Eggs, Kisi me slowly, gently or Potatoland. Their labels feature geishas, riot scenes, make reference to Playboy and other bold, artistic imagery. They’re colourful, vibrant, modern, and beautifully designed. Sometimes they give you almost no information; other times, they give you every little detail. They’re often bottled in clear glass to show off the wine’s hue, sealed with crown caps or other quirky closures, or dipped in brightly coloured wax. Of course I’d pick that over Château Boring.

Maybe all the money saved in the winery is simply spent on branding instead?

I put that question to Neil Tully MW, founder of Amphora Design, a wine branding and design agency based in Bath. His answer was no, they don’t spend more, with one important caveat: the design proposals tend to be bolder, and the branding decisions are far more intentional.

(As it turns out, making natural wine isn’t necessarily cheaper.)

Tully also suggested that winemakers in more ‘serious’ wine regions may not feel they have the same freedom, especially when it comes to the judgement of their peers. Perhaps natural wine producers aren’t as burdened by the need to be taken seriously—to make a “serious” wine capable of earning high scores. Perhaps it reflects the personalities of the winemakers themselves: people who are rule-breakers, who push boundaries. I think it’s all of the above — and more.
A beautifully plated dish from a Michelin-starred restaurant immediately looks more desirable than a rustic plate of pasta. We eat with our eyes first. But wine is different. Pour a glass of a great wine beside a glass of good wine and, in identical glasses, they will look much the same. The quality cannot be seen. That’s why, before the cork is pulled, the label has already done most of the selling.

And it doesn’t even have to be a “radical” label. When I was selling wine online in China, we put this to the test. We sold exactly the same Côtes du Rhône AOC from the same domaine, the same vintage, and the same wine—only the label was different. One bottle carried the producer’s regular label; the other featured a special “Centenary” label. Guess which one sold twice as much? We ran a similar experiment with Riesling. These weren’t identical wines, but they were comparable in quality, provenance, and style—both were off-dry Rieslings, but one had a blue bottle. Our blue-bottle Riesling outsold the other by three to one. These are only small examples from a very small business, so I wouldn’t pretend they’re scientifically rigorous. But they illustrate something that anyone who has sold wine to consumers already knows: design matters more than the liquid that’s inside the bottle. Sad? Perhaps. True? Yes.

We discussed sulphites already, but there’s a broader point here: the word natural does a great deal of work on its own. Type “natural wine” into Google and one of the first suggested searches is, “Is natural wine actually better for you?” Whether we like it or not, natural carries a promise — the rejection of “harsh chemicals”, the halo of sustainable viticulture — that resonates with consumers. If it’s natural, the logic goes, it must be good for me, or at least better for me. Well — see sulphites above. But even if consumers have been misguided (by whom is a discussion for another day), that doesn’t mean the rest of the wine industry should ignore the message. Consumers are telling us what they want: wines they perceive to be more sustainable, less industrial and, above all, healthier.

Speaking to Chris Boiling — a winemaker who only makes what his labels literally call “Crazy Experimental Wines,” in very small batches across Slovenia, Hungary, Georgia and Austria (soon Albania too) — told me he named one of his wines Oh, Natural! because, yes, he expected it to attract more interest from the market. Not to mention that his labels (done by the team at Amphora Design) go all out on radical transparency, letting you in on every step of the winemaking process — and even some of the viticulture — which I find refreshing, when all you’re normally given is the usual boilerplate story that adds little value to the end consumer.

As we’ve seen, the word natural can be interpreted as a move away from ultra-processed wine, in keeping with the wider health and sustainability discourse. It can also signal a move away from large corporations in favour of smaller, more thoughtful producers. And this isn’t unique to wine. We’ve seen the same trend in craft beer and gin. Inventive, original labels stand in stark contrast to the corporate branding of the likes of Stella Artois or Heineken, inviting consumers to choose something that feels small-batch, independent and distinctive — even if many of those brands have, in fact, been quietly hoovered up by multinationals. The lesson isn’t that we should mislead consumers, but that, once again, they’ve spoken. They’ve voted against the perceived sameness of big brands and the industrialisation of food and drink, and in favour of products that feel independent, distinctive and full of personality.

The places where these beers, wines and gins are sold also tend to be younger, more welcoming and more relaxed than those where you’ll typically find more traditional wines. If I were to stereotype, a classic wine bar is where you might take a date; a natural wine bar is where you’d meet your mates. Perhaps it’s simply the sort of environment that’s more conducive to relaxing around wine.

Another topic I discussed with Neil Tully: he feels that, even in the way labels are designed, natural wine places more emphasis on the wine itself than on the denomination. Having recently been in Burgundy, a traditional producer mentioned that on their Grand Cru wines, the appellation and the climat would be written in a larger font than the producer’s logo, because much of the wine’s identity is owed to the terroir, which in fact seems to support Tully’s point.

The last thing I want to mention is taste and smell. This is pure speculation on my part, but I wonder whether the kombucha-like flavours so often associated with natural wines reinforce their perceived healthiness through flavour associations alone. Even though, like Chris Boiling or Gravner, many natural winemakers place great emphasis on producing clean wines (sometimes using small amounts of sulphur dioxide to achieve that), those savoury, fermented aromas may subconsciously signal “natural”, “alive” or “healthy” to consumers. I also wonder whether their more pungent, distinctive aroma s— rather like unpasteurised cheese — give less wine-experienced drinkers the confidence that they’re actually tasting something, that they’re participating in the ritual of wine tasting. Faced with a more subtle wine, perhaps they wouldn’t feel quite so sure?

Of course, slapping a two-finger salute on the label of a fifth-generation family estate won’t translate well, if at all. But the lesson isn’t to imitate natural wine; it’s to understand what it has understood about consumers. They want clarity over jargon, transparency over marketing clichés, personality over corporate polish, and a clearer sense of what a wine will actually offer them before they buy it — not afterwards. Above all, they want wine to feel less intimidating and more fun. If the rest of the wine industry can embrace those lessons without abandoning its own identity, it may have a better chance of persuading the next generation to drink wine at all.

Photo by Peter Neumann on Unsplash

title: Too Difficult?
summary: Yeats entitled one of his mid-life poems ‘The Fascination of What’s Difficult’. The poem is mainly a complaint, about the tangled business of running a theatre (the Abbey in Dublin) and the infuriating difficulty of “management of men”, as opposed to the pure delight of writing poetry. But the title points to something which has […]
content:
Yeats entitled one of his mid-life poems ‘The Fascination of What’s Difficult’. The poem is mainly a complaint, about the tangled business of running a theatre (the Abbey in Dublin) and the infuriating difficulty of “management of men”, as opposed to the pure delight of writing poetry. But the title points to something which has impelled the poet to get involved in areas that pose intractable problems. And he doesn’t mention, at least in this poem, the great satisfactions that founding and running the theatre which staged JM Synge’s masterpiece Playboy of the Western World also afforded. Did Yeats really regret all that – even though, as you may remember, the first performances of Playboy led to riots? I don’t think so.

I’ve been pondering the fascination of difficult wines. This may not seem a very appealing subject, and somehow reminds me of those courses you can take in “Dealing with difficult people”. But let’s turn things around. If you don’t like the sound of difficult wines, surely the thought of “easy-drinking wines” is much more horrific.

An “easy-drinking” wine is a wine that can offend nobody; a wine from which nearly every trace of character, of specific style and origin, has been removed. We all know the kind of thing: those bland, expressionless Pinot Grigios and Merlots which are served in Economy Class or in hotel lobbies, and are the vinous equivalent of those environments. Those environments are also the natural home of another aesthetic horror, “easy-listening music”.

But a “difficult-drinking” wine? That hardly sounds like a winning marketing formula, any more than “difficult-to-listen-to music”. Let’s delve deeper into the concept.

Difficult wines, like difficult people, can be “in your face”. They don’t hold back, they say what they think, they are what they are. They implicitly challenge you to take them or leave them. One thing they will not be is bland and inoffensive.

Take Greece’s Assyrtiko. Never was a grape variety better named. Assyrtiko is assertive bordering on aggressive. It bristles with acidity, but balances that with texture and volume. When I was helping choose wines for my tennis club, and introduced an Assyrtiko, it divided opinion more sharply than any other wine on the list. One member complained it gave him migraines. But for those who persevere, Assyrtiko brings huge rewards. For me it is not just Greece’s most interesting grape variety, but one of the most fascinating varieties on the planet.

“Difficult” wines, like difficult music, for example the serialism originally developed by Schoenberg, may pose a kind of intellectual or epistemological puzzle – a difficulty of understanding. This has been my experience with two types of wines in particular, orange wines and the Nebbiolo-based reds of Piedmont.

When faced with a range of wines made by the dean of orange wine (or amber wine as he prefers to call it), Joska Gravner of Friuli, I was initially baffled. These austere ferments lacked most of the qualities I look for in wine, especially white wine: where were the primary fruit notes, where was the florality which is a feature of certain grapes varieties (Viognier, Gewürztraminer, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Bacchus etc), where was, more generally, the enticing charm?

These wines did not initially speak to me, or if they were speaking, I was not conversant with their language. I remember commenting that they seemed to require a whole new wine writing vocabulary. But with time, and further tasting, I began to get the hang of Gravner’s very particular approach to winemaking, based, he told me, not on modern scientific methods but on the Roman viticulturalist Columella. I found they had a certain gravitas and solemnity, not unlike the character of the gnomic Sr Gravner himself.

My puzzlement with the Nebbiolo-based wines of Piedmont was similar, though less radical. These were traditionally made red wines, but it was the character of Nebbiolo itself which eluded me. That combination of palish, Pinot Noir-ish colour with a tannic structure more reminiscent of Cabernet Sauvignon, the absence of berry fruit aromas and flavours, tantalising suggestions of earth and smoke…I was puzzled, I had been set a challenge, but it was one I wanted to explore. Part of the solution was setting aside preconceptions based on classic French red wines. There’s no point approaching Stravinsky, say, and expecting his music to sound like Brahms.

Sherry is another wine, or family of wines, which many find “difficult.” The difficulty doubtless comes from two features of sherry, the deliberate oxidation and dramatically higher levels of the pungent chemical acetaldehyde than are found in other wines. It’s quite natural to be put off by acetaldehyde – perhaps in the same kind of way that a naïve listener might be initially put off by the spiky intervals and absence of conventional harmonies in Schönberg, Berg or Webern. But both with sherry and with 12-tone music, if you’re prepared to open that mental door and keep going, you will be in for some wonderful experiences.

Facing up to disruptive audience members during the initial run of Playboy, apparently offended by references to women’s underwear but more likely by the unflattering portrayal of Irish manhood, Yeats defended artistic freedom and more specifically Synge’s right to show social realities on stage. Later in an interview he said “as far as [I] could see the people who formed the opposition had no books in their houses.” We can all react defensively when faced with the unfamiliar, whether it’s an unsparing dramatic masterpiece or a wine outside our comfort zone. But it’s surely better to stay with it, if we can; acknowledge our initial bewilderment but not react against it; begin to learn.

Photo by Karla Hernandez on Unsplash

title: The Manipulation of Nature
summary: Why are there so many exclamation marks in the world, and so few hyphens? What spurred this reflection was a menu: a dish featuring ‘Grilled line caught John Dory fillet’. And an unrelated Instagram post enthusing about exclamation marks! They’re such fun!! Aren’t they!?! Well. Exclamation marks are generally unnecessary and mostly silly. Hyphens are […]
content:
Why are there so many exclamation marks in the world, and so few hyphens?

What spurred this reflection was a menu: a dish featuring ‘Grilled line caught John Dory fillet’. And an unrelated Instagram post enthusing about exclamation marks! They’re such fun!! Aren’t they!?!

Well. Exclamation marks are generally unnecessary and mostly silly. Hyphens are essential for clarifying meaning. In that hyphenless dish, the reader infers that the fish was line-caught, rather than caught by a grilled line; but we infer it because it’s the most likely meaning. It’s not what it says, but common sense tells us that’s what we should infer.

In wine, how much is inferred and how much is clearly conveyed? When Vignoble des Cabottes says that it now has one vineyard worker for every 1.6 hectares, compared to the one per 3.6 ha it used to have, you think, gosh, that’s good. Vineyard workers are like exclamation marks, for those who like them – the more the merrier!!! We infer careful work, attention to detail. But winery workers are like hyphens: one, or maybe none – who knows? – suggests minimal intervention, and that is good, because it conveys the meaning of the vineyard more clearly. Surely?

But what is that meaning that we want to hear and taste so clearly? Go to the Whistler show at Tate Britain and you will see evocative scenes of the Thames at twilight, or at night. Yes, you will say – that’s just what it looks like. But it’s not, because the picture is a swish and a blob, and from that you infer all the detail you have seen for yourself, in the flesh. Painting, and not just Impressionism, relies on inference. Zurbaran, in a show at the National Gallery, paints fabrics you can feel: you infer the texture, the heft so clearly that your fingers almost tingle. Look closely, though, and has he actually painted the stitches, the weave? No. Not remotely. It’s called art.

We all – critics, wine-lovers – say we want to see the place reflected in the wine. Good tasters can work backwards, in a blind tasting, to identify the place from the taste. Pedro Parra, soil consultant extraordinaire, identifies the soil type from the flavour and then runs through the places he knows with that soil. (So his colleague Alberto Antonini tells me.) And we all know there are all sorts of things that obstruct that clear conveyance of information: overripeness, underripeness, too high yields, too low yields, too much winemaking, too  little winemaking, aromatic yeasts, too much oak… it’s a long list.

And it brings to mind the old question of whether wine is art or science. Whistler was clear that ‘Nature is very seldom right’; he reckoned the best plein-air painting was done back in the studio, and he used many different techniques to achieve his effects: artifice to convey truth.

Wine relies on colossal artifice, dressed up as Nature. Vineyards are not natural. Growers now want to recreate a natural, biodiverse universe in their essentially unnatural vineyards, but it’s a universe of their choice, not one where phylloxera, esca and downy mildew gang up to slaughter their vines and return those hectares to natural brambles and nettles. The place the winemaker wants you to see via the wine is the place the winemaker sees or imagines: the contours, the subsoil, the bedrock, the rain and the wind and the sun. Some of these, things beneath the surface, are largely unseen. From an English sparkling you must infer the chalk and the flint and the dew and the hedgerows, the skylarks and the blackcaps – never mind that a friend in Tillington in Sussex tells me (anecdotally) that since the great expansion of vineyards there most bird life has lessened. Most winegrowers, if they’re honest, must admit that they’re with Whistler when it comes to Nature, even if some of them now are prepared to make sacrifices to get those skylarks and blackcaps back.

As an aside, I have just visited a Welsh vineyard of which none of this is true: Paul Rolt grows his vines (Solaris and Rondo) at Hebron in Carmarthenshire up willow trees: the soil is never broken, the grass and docks and red campion grow waist-high, and the vines even higher to form arched pergolas overhead along the trained willow branches. Willows, he says, work with both endomycorrhizal and ectomycorrhizal fungi in the soil, whereas vines only work with endo endomycorrhizal fungi; those, and the grasses, and the insects and the birds (plenty of them, by the way) form a proper ecosystem. Does it reflect the site more precisely than bare soil and avian silence? It’s certainly intended to. I would love to taste the results of such viticulture from, say Riesling or Pinot Noir, on sites known to give a particular character.

The manipulation of nature makes winegrowers artists, does it not? Art is ruthless. Nice, gentle, sweet, it is not. (I remember a weekend painter saying to my artist husband, ‘Oh, painting is so relaxing, isn’t it? He was too dumbfounded to answer.)

Winemakers, you might say, want you to do more than infer place in their wine: they want to convey it clearly, punctuation and all. Growers in Sancerre say they don’t make Sauvignon Blanc; they make Sancerre. Some even do. Even if they say they stand back and become invisible, they chose the grapes; they decided if the wine would be still or sparkling or pét-nat; they decided what fermentation vessel to use, and when to bottle. They’re still doing a Whistler: they’re still correcting nature in order to portray her more accurately, even if they do spend a lot of time listening to her first.

All the hyphens are in place. In food, do they matter so much? They don’t affect the flavour of the dish, though they might affect what you expect on your plate. ‘Skin on chicken breast’, for example, is faintly unsettling.

Photo by Rishabh Dharmani on Unsplash

title: The Judgment of Paris Revisited
summary: Even for opera lovers, it promises to be an odd show. Next month’s Napa Valley Festival stages the premiere of a work bringing Bacchus and Venus to 1970s Paris and Napa, mythological heroes re-enacting the wine world’s most mythical tasting. The Judgment of Paris, the opera, is the latest re-telling of the celebrated 1976 tasting […]
content:
Even for opera lovers, it promises to be an odd show. Next month’s Napa Valley Festival stages the premiere of a work bringing Bacchus and Venus to 1970s Paris and Napa, mythological heroes re-enacting the wine world’s most mythical tasting. The Judgment of Paris, the opera, is the latest re-telling of the celebrated 1976 tasting pitting Californian wines against Bordeaux’s most illustrious names. And while it surely can’t be artistically any worse than Bottle Shock, the 2008 comedy-drama telling the same tale (Alan Rickman played Steven Spurrier) it promises to be every bit as smugly tedious.

Last month brought a rash of such commemorations, prompted by 24 May’s 50th anniversary of the contest. You might have thought that after half a century, red-trousered wine merchants and writers would pipe down about it. You’d be wrong, because this is one of the few times they’ve ever impinged on popular consciousness (at least as represented by New York Times and Guardian readers) and they’re not letting us forget it.

I won’t deny the deliciousness of blazered Bordelais aristocrats and wine experts who’d never deigned to taste non-French wines being made to look silly. “Ah, back to France!” one judge reportedly exclaimed as he tasted a Napa Chardonnay. Judge Odette Kahn, then editor of La Revue du Vin de France, famously tried to get her scorecard back to hide the fact that she had ranked Stag’s Leap Cab 1973 and Mayacamas Vineyards Cab 1971 first and second, ahead of the likes of Châteaux Mouton-Rothschild and Haut-Brion. Though the French press avoided any mention of the event at the time, a few months later Le Figaro described the results as “laughable”. Except, unlike the Californians, they weren’t laughing.

In 1976 – especially for Time’s George Taber, the only reporter to attend – it was a great story. Fifty years on, even considering the wine world and its writers’ lack of news sense, not so much.  Regular re-enactments of the tasting since, using more mature vintages, haven’t revived its news value. And in part, this is simply because the Judgment of Paris changed so little.

Of course it was a boon to Californian wine. California’s industry in the early 1970s was still dominated by dire jug wines: Napa’s production of dry red wines overtook that of sweet ones only in the late 1960s. For the pioneers who triumphed in Paris, the effect was immediate. Soon after, Chateau Montelena winemaker Mike Grgich won backing to start his own Grgich Hills winery: years later, he told Business Week that “My life is divided into two parts – before the Paris tasting and after.” Elsewhere, the result put rockets under what was already a growing wave of investment: California’s land under vines tripled between 1964 and 1984.

Out in the rest of wine’s New World, there was no doubt some ripple effect. But not much: those countries and producers made their own luck. In Australia in the 1970s, technological innovations (especially temperature control) and changing domestic tastes were far more important that the Paris result. New Zealand had barely even begun planting yet. Argentina already had a substantial industry based on domestic consumption. Chile faced a crisis in domestic sales under Pinochet’s dictatorship, which it exported its way out of in the 1980s. South Africa’s industry remained cut off from the world by apartheid for years to come.

And back in Bordeaux, so dramatically humbled by Stag’s Leap et al? The Judgment of Paris had no impact at all. Indeed, powered by better winemaking techniques and, ironically, an American cheerleader, Robert Parker, Bordeaux’s elite scaled new heights of fame and wealth. The storied 1982 vintage both made Parker and marked the start of a new golden age for Bordeaux’s higher-end winemakers. From this point they were able to sell unfinished wine en primeur, such was the demand for it – an arrogant bit of cashflow management that most winemakers could only dream of getting away with. And far from shunning claret for homegrown stars, America accounted for up to 15% of 1980s Bordeaux exports.

Nor, except for Californian wines sold in the US, did the world beyond France make real inroads into the fine wine market in the following decades. In Australia, Henschke and Penfolds were already making iconic wines and forged their own path. In South America, premium fine-wine brands didn’t emerge until Concha y Toro’s Don Melchor (1987), with the likes of Seña, Almaviva and Cheval des Andes following a decade or more later.

Indeed in 2000, when former stockbrokers James Miles and Justin Gibbs launched Liv-ex, Bordeaux remained commercially the only fine-wine game in town. Liv-Ex’s benchmark Fine Wine 50 index continues to track only the most heavily-traded fine wines: Bordeaux First Growths. Even in 2010, Bordeaux represented 95% of the global secondary fine-wine market. Aside from a handful of Piemonte and Tuscan stars and scattered curiosities (Tokaj, Vega Sicilia), few non-French wines disturbed the fine-wine lists of St James’s Street. So much for Paris 1976.

There has indeed been a vinous revolution in the past 15 years: partly thanks to the sea change in wine quality around the world since the turn of the century – and in part because of Bordeaux’s hubris. A combination of economic crises and the greed of the top châteaux has brought the en primeur system to the brink of collapse. The consensus at this point seems to be that this year’s campaign isn’t as disastrous as 2025’s. But as Wine-Searcher reported last week, “Bordeaux [retail] prices are dropping dramatically” in the US. Today the region represents only around a third of the global secondary fine-wine market.

The Judgment of Paris was a vital moment for Californian wine. But it made little difference to anyone else – least of all the merchants and auction houses poised to make a bigger killing than ever in Bordeaux. We all love a plucky upstart’s moment of glory. But ultimately, as in society at large, the red trousers won – which is why they celebrate it.

Photo by Sasun Bughdaryan on Unsplash
 
Andrew Neather blogs at https://aviewfrommytable.substack.com/

title: Looking Back
summary: Twice a year, I help to organise a wine dinner for a group of friends. For the most recent one, in Paris, my job was to bring the sweet wines and a selection of Grenaches. In preparation, I looked at what I have in bond and had a selection delivered to my house. Coravin in […]
content:
Twice a year, I help to organise a wine dinner for a group of friends. For the most recent one, in Paris, my job was to bring the sweet wines and a selection of Grenaches. In preparation, I looked at what I have in bond and had a selection delivered to my house. Coravin in hand, I set to work.

A three-vintage selection of Domaine Huet Vouvray Moelleux sorted the stickies in minutes. The reds were trickier. I lined up two Châteauneuf-du-Papes, a Gigondas and a Cannonau Di Sardegna, all of which were at least ten years’ old. One – a 2009 Le Vieux Donjon – was delicious. The others were “stuffed” as they like to say in Australia. I’d kept them all too long, paying storage costs to hang onto wines that were well past their best.

My experience got me thinking about old wines in general. Why do we keep them? What do we expect when we pull the cork? Is it a way of indulging the British tendency to covet disappointment? I’m an enthusiastic member of the DIY (Drink It Young) club, but even I must admit that the majority of the most memorable wines I’ve drunk over the last 40 years have been mature ones.

Old wines can be supremely enjoyable and come with an extra cachet if they are rare. On occasion, there’s a degree of self-satisfaction, even humble bragging, involved, which is why people are so quick to share their experiences on Instagram. But can they teach us something? Do they make us more informed tasters?

I’ve attended a couple of tastings in the last month that have done just that. The first was an vertical of 20 years of Palladius, the top white from South Africa’s most accomplished winemaker, Eben Sadie, right back to 2003, put on by Berry Brothers.

Inspired by Eben’s love of white Rhônes and his time in Priorat, Palladius was the first Mediterranean Cape blend. “I was almost stoned for doing it,” he remembers. The early vintages were patchy, but it was fascinating to see the blend and Eben’s approach evolve with the years. At the start, it contained Chenin Blanc, Chardonnay, Grenache Blanc and Viognier and 25% new wood. Little by little, other, mostly more acidic grapes were added: Clairette Blanche (2007), Verdelho (2011), Marsanne (2014), Colombard (2105), Picpoul, Vermentino, Grillo and Cinsault Blanc (2019) and Assyrtiko (2021). From 2014, Eben did away with barrels. Today Palladius is a sublime, 14-variety assemblage.

The tasting was educational because it allowed us to follow the palate and evolving thought process of one the world’s most talented winemakers. It gave us a glimpse into what Sadie calls “a deeper sense of time”. The early years, as I’ve said, were hit and miss. The most recent vintage – the 2023 – is the best and most complex Palladius yet.

The second tasting was a very different occasion, put on Pedro Peciña in Logroño. As well as making wine under his own El Vino Pródigo label, Pedro buys and sells venerable bottles of mostly Spanish wine from restaurants, collectors, widows and distressed bodegas as part of his La Guarida del Pródigo business. For years, he’s been offering to open a few of them for me. Last week, he made good on the promise, lining up more than 20 bottles from Rioja, Ribera del Duero, Jerez, Navarra and the Napa Valley.

Given that Pedro lives and works in the region – and has good connections there – three quarters of the wines were from Rioja, right back to a Viña Pomal 1953. Among other things, we tasted a CVNE Imperial 1962, a Rioja Alta 904 1968, a Muga Prado Enea 1969, a López de Heredia Viña Bosconia 1973, a Marqués de Riscal 1981, a Marqués de Murrieta 1982, a Remelluri 1983 and a Viña Real 1987. The quality of these older wines was very high, only let down by the occasional faulty cork and one instance of Brett. No other region in the world, not even Burgundy, could match the complexity and longevity on show.

But what really made the tasting so special was the discussion among the nine people who were privileged to attend. All of us know a lot about Rioja, but no one was attempting to boast or show off about that knowledge. We wanted to understand the vintages, the house styles, the blends and the way Rioja has changed in the intervening years. Old wines can be great, but it’s the people you share them with that really matter.
